Databases and SQL: from records to reliable changes

6 sequenced activities with worked examples, independent practice and an equipment-free route.

Student PDFOffline student pack & filesTeacher answers

Before starting: Teach in the numbered order. Activities 01-04 establish the Year 11 pathway; 05 introduces grouped reports with a labelled Year 12 HAVING extension. Complete relevant practice and feedback before any assessment. This is a progression, not a claim to cover every SQL syllabus item.

Suggested 55-minute lesson: 8 minutes textbook reading, 12 modelling, 20 independent practice, 10 feedback and 5 exit reflection. Adapt after classroom trial. Keep predictions separate from observed results. Paper traces are valid practice but do not prove that software or equipment ran.

2026 foundation · 2027 revisions. Public, ungraded formative practice; answers are on a separate page. No student responses are collected. Optional specialist equipment can supply a context after the general task; it is not required.

Follow the full SQL learning pathway for the Year 11 / Year 12 sequence, changed databases, expected results and assessment readiness. This condensed pack mixes foundations with later material: Activity 05 grouped reports belong after the Year 11 whole-result aggregate work; its HAVING task is a supporting extension.

01 · Model records before querying

Read, predict and model

Name __________________ Class ______ Date __________

Textbook visit: Read the linked chapter. Return to its worked examples before trying the independent task.

Use this synthetic dataset throughout the pack. returned is 1 for returned and 0 for outstanding. days is a stored duration, not a live date calculation. Loan.member_id refers to Member.member_id; one member may have zero or many loans. Each loan belongs to exactly one member.

Member IDName
1Ari
2Bo
3Cleo
Loan IDMember IDItemDaysReturned
1011Camera31
1021Headset50
1032Camera21
1042Tripod50

member_id uniquely identifies a member. A name is not a reliable key: two people can share it. Separating member details avoids changing the same name on every loan.

Equipment-free route

Use the printed tables as record cards. Draw keys and relationships on paper; apply integrity rules manually. Keep these tables beside later SQL activities.

Explain and transfer

Annotate one step of the worked example in your own words. Change one supplied input, record a new prediction and show how the rule produces it. Label a hand trace separately from a software observation.

02 · Select columns and specify order

Read, predict and model

Name __________________ Class ______ Date __________

Textbook visit: Read the linked chapter. Return to its worked examples before trying the independent task.

SQL returns a table. SELECT chooses output columns, FROM chooses source records, and ORDER BY specifies the result order. Without ORDER BY, do not rely on the displayed order. Run setup.sql once in a fresh SQLite database if using software.

SELECT loan_id, item
FROM Loan
ORDER BY loan_id;
loan_iditem
101Camera
102Headset
103Camera
104Tripod

The query returns four rows; item alone is not unique. SELECT DISTINCT item FROM Loan ORDER BY item; returns Camera, Headset, Tripod.

Equipment-free route

Write the SQL and construct the result table by hand from Activity 01. Label it a manual result; a school-approved SQLite tool is optional.

Explain and transfer

Annotate one step of the worked example in your own words. Change one supplied input, record a new prediction and show how the rule produces it. Label a hand trace separately from a software observation.

03 · Filter rows and test boundaries

Read, predict and model

Name __________________ Class ______ Date __________

Textbook visit: Read the linked chapter. Return to its worked examples before trying the independent task.

WHERE filters individual rows before the result is sorted. BETWEEN includes both endpoints. Text literals use single quotes. Parentheses make combined conditions explicit.

SELECT loan_id, item, days
FROM Loan
WHERE returned = 0 AND days BETWEEN 3 AND 5
ORDER BY loan_id;

The result is (102, Headset, 5) and (104, Tripod, 5). Test the boundary separately: a returned = 0 row with days = 3 would also qualify. This dataset does not by itself demonstrate that lower boundary.

Equipment-free route

Evaluate the Boolean expression on each printed row. Use separate true/false columns for its parts and construct the final table without database software.

Explain and transfer

Annotate one step of the worked example in your own words. Change one supplied input, record a new prediction and show how the rule produces it. Label a hand trace separately from a software observation.

04 · Join related records without losing meaning

Read, predict and model

Name __________________ Class ______ Date __________

Textbook visit: Read the linked chapter. Return to its worked examples before trying the independent task.

A join pairs related rows. The ON clause must match the member identifier, not loan_id. A member with two loans produces two result rows; that is expected one-to-many behaviour.

SELECT Member.name, Loan.loan_id, Loan.item
FROM Member INNER JOIN Loan
ON Member.member_id = Loan.member_id
ORDER BY Loan.loan_id;

The result is Ari/101/Camera, Ari/102/Headset, Bo/103/Camera, Bo/104/Tripod. Cleo is absent because an INNER JOIN requires a matching loan.

Equipment-free route

Place matching Member and Loan cards beside one another. Construct each joined output row by hand; include a no-match card for Cleo.

Explain and transfer

Annotate one step of the worked example in your own words. Change one supplied input, record a new prediction and show how the rule produces it. Label a hand trace separately from a software observation.

04 · Join related records without losing meaning

Independent practice and evidence

Name __________________ Class ______ Date __________

A. Independent report

Write a joined report listing member name, loan_id and item only for outstanding loans. Order by loan_id and predict every row.

B. Diagnose a faulty join

A learner joins ON Member.member_id = Loan.loan_id. Predict the row count here and explain the error. Another learner omits the matching condition entirely and produces every member-loan pair: calculate that row count.

Exit / later extension

Why does counting joined rows fail to count distinct members? After INNER JOIN is secure, investigate LEFT JOIN: which extra member would it preserve, and what would the missing Loan columns contain?

05 · Aggregate first, then filter groups

Read, predict and model

Name __________________ Class ______ Date __________

Textbook visit: Read the linked chapter. Return to its worked examples before trying the independent task.

Start with one table. GROUP BY partitions rows by a chosen key. COUNT(*) counts rows in each group and SUM(days) adds stored durations. Every selected non-aggregate column here is grouped. These rules avoid SQLite-specific bare-column behaviour.

SELECT member_id, COUNT(*) AS loans, SUM(days) AS total_days
FROM Loan
GROUP BY member_id
ORDER BY member_id;

Result: (1, 2, 8), (2, 2, 7). Cleo has no Loan rows, so no group appears. AVG(days) over all four loans is 15 / 4 = 3.75; COUNT(*) is 4.

Equipment-free route

Sort printed loan cards into piles by the grouping key and calculate each aggregate. Use the optional extension only after feedback on Activity 04 and the grouped report.

Explain and transfer

Annotate one step of the worked example in your own words. Change one supplied input, record a new prediction and show how the rule produces it. Label a hand trace separately from a software observation.

05 · Aggregate first, then filter groups

Independent practice and evidence

Name __________________ Class ______ Date __________

A. Independent grouped report

Group by item, showing item, COUNT(*) and MAX(days), ordered by item. Predict each row. Then add WHERE returned = 0 before GROUP BY and recalculate.

B. Year 12 extension: HAVING

After grouped reports are secure, return member_id and SUM(days) only for groups whose sum is at least 8. Use HAVING SUM(days) >= 8. Explain why WHERE SUM(days) >= 8 is unsuitable here.

Exit

For a LEFT JOIN from Member to Loan, why would COUNT(Loan.loan_id) give Cleo zero while COUNT(*) gives one? Refer to the preserved unmatched row.

06 · Make controlled changes and prove the result

Read, predict and model

Name __________________ Class ______ Date __________

Textbook visit: Read the linked chapter. Return to its worked examples before trying the independent task.

Work only on a disposable copy. In each SQLite connection, run PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; before BEGIN and check PRAGMA foreign_keys; returns 1. This setting is not saved in the database file. A transaction groups changes until COMMIT makes them persistent or ROLLBACK cancels them. Preview the target row before changing it. The example marks loan 102 returned, checks it, then rolls back.

BEGIN;
SELECT loan_id, returned FROM Loan WHERE loan_id = 102;
UPDATE Loan SET returned = 1 WHERE loan_id = 102;
SELECT loan_id, returned FROM Loan WHERE loan_id = 102;
ROLLBACK;

Before: (102,0). Inside transaction: (102,1). After ROLLBACK a fresh SELECT gives (102,0). An UPDATE without WHERE would change all four rows.

Equipment-free route

Use a second paper copy of the tables. Pencil in changes, record before/after rows, then discard the copy for rollback. This models effects but does not prove a database engine enforced a constraint.

Explain and transfer

Annotate one step of the worked example in your own words. Change one supplied input, record a new prediction and show how the rule produces it. Label a hand trace separately from a software observation.

06 · Make controlled changes and prove the result

Independent practice and evidence

Name __________________ Class ______ Date __________

A. Independent transaction

In a fresh copy, insert Member (4, 'Dev'), then Loan (105, 4, 'Light', 1, 0). Preview and delete only loan 105. Verify Member 4 still exists, then ROLLBACK the whole transaction. Predict final row counts. Write every statement.

B. Create and test a constraint

Write CREATE TABLE Tag with tag_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and label TEXT NOT NULL. In a separate scratch database, predict the outcome of inserting (1, NULL), then (1, Light) with the text correctly quoted. Explain what the two constraints protect.

Exit

List the evidence you would retain before committing an authorised change. Explain why running the same insert twice can fail.
